scope.definition: Architecture for coordinating multiple software-building or maintenance agents: intake/routing, durable scheduling, workflow state, retries, short/long-term memory, event transport, supervision, human approval, observability, and recovery. An agent is a model-driven decision component; the control plane is deterministic infrastructure that owns authorization and lifecycle. A durable workflow engine is distinct from an in-process agent conversation framework.
scope.included: Issue-to-plan-to-patch/test/review/merge/deploy/remediate flows; centralized supervisors, explicit graphs, blackboard/event-driven workers, and hybrid single/multi-agent routing; interoperability through MCP (agent-to-tool) and A2A (agent-to-agent).
scope.excluded: Model training and detailed coding-agent quality except where orchestration evidence depends on them.

current_state.claim: Production-grade deterministic primitives already exist: persisted event history/state, worker queues, leases, retries/backoff, timeouts, compensation, and event triggers. Temporal records history for crash recovery [S1-S5]; Kubernetes controllers reconcile desired and actual state [S15-S16]; AWS and Prefect expose explicit retry policies [S18-S19,S26].
Agent frameworks now expose graph routing, checkpoints, handoffs, interrupts/human-in-loop, stores, and tracing [S6-S13]. A2A 1.0 standardizes discovery and remote asynchronous task exchange [S14].

The reliable architecture is therefore a conventional distributed workflow/control plane containing probabilistic agents, not an LLM supervisor acting as its own scheduler/database/security boundary. The inference follows from delivery and replay semantics [S3-S5,S17-S19] and documented MAS failures [S20].
No neutral, cross-framework evidence establishes end-to-end unattended issue-to-production reliability, total cost, or safety for long-lived multi-agent software projects.

systems: Temporal (event-sourced durable workflows, task queues, retries)
AWS Step Functions Standard/Express (managed state machines)

representative_systems.note: A broker transports events; it does not replace workflow history, joins, compensation, or policy.

systems: Microsoft Agent Framework 1.0 (successor to AutoGen; workflows/checkpoint/HITL/telemetry)
AutoGen (maintenance mode as of access, so migrate rather than start new)
A2A 1.0 for remote agent discovery/task lifecycle
MCP for tools/context, with explicit security hazards

primary_evidence: Temporal explicitly persists append-only workflow event history used for recovery, has worker-polled task queues, and defaults failed Activities to declarative retries [S1-S3]. It also documents hard history limits and at-least-once Activity execution, proving that durability still requires Continue-As-New/history management and idempotent effects [S4,S5].

LangGraph separates thread checkpoints from cross-thread stores and warns that RAM savers lose state and checkpoints grow without retention [S6]. Its own multi-agent guide says single-agent designs can often suffice [S7].

Microsoft's repository declares AutoGen maintenance mode and MAF 1.0 its production-ready successor; MAF documents graph workflows, checkpointing, streaming, human-in-loop, time travel, OpenTelemetry, and a separate durable extension [S8-S10]. This supports capability/status only, not independent reliability.
OpenAI SDK handoffs are tools selected by the model; its boundary guardrails and tracing are useful but guardrails can race with model work and ZDR disables OpenAI-hosted tracing [S11-S13].

A2A 1.0 defines Agent Cards and async tasks with polling, SSE streaming, push notification, artifacts, input-required state, authentication, and opaque execution [S14]. It standardizes the wire contract, not scheduler reliability, authorization policy, or agent correctness.

NATS documents at-least-once persistent delivery, while AWS distinguishes Standard exactly-once state execution claims from Express at-least-once execution [S17-S19]. These differences require an explicit delivery contract rather than assuming exactly once.

MCP's security guidance enumerates confused deputy, token passthrough, SSRF, local compromise, session hijacking, and minimal-scope concerns [S23]; GitHub documents both rich event triggers and the danger of untrusted input/secrets in workflows [S24,S25].

independent_evidence.finding: MAST studied 1,600+ annotated traces from seven MAS frameworks. Its taxonomy found 14 modes across system-design, inter-agent-misalignment, and task-verification categories; taxonomy validation reports kappa 0.88. Authors say gains on popular benchmarks are often minimal [S20].
independent_evidence.caveat: Preprint; trace selection, frameworks, tasks, and judge pipeline limit generalization, but human agreement and released taxonomy make it strong diagnostic evidence.

independent_evidence.finding: A 2025 empirical comparison reports that MAS advantage shrinks as base models improve; its hybrid SAS/MAS cascade improved tested accuracy by 1.1-12% and cut deployment cost by up to 20% [S21].
independent_evidence.caveat: Preprint and workload-specific; percentage ranges should not be projected to software maintenance without replication.

independent_evidence.finding: Agent Forest reports sampling-and-voting accuracy scaling with more agents [S22].
independent_evidence.caveat: This supports parallel independent sampling plus aggregation under tested benchmarks, not conversational role-play, durable operations, or monotonic value after latency/token costs.

independent_evidence.synthesis: Evidence conflicts only superficially: parallel diversity and voting can help hard tasks [S22], while unconstrained collaboration introduces coordination/verification failures [S20] and strong single agents narrow the gap [S21]. Route selectively and require measurable marginal value.

metrics.value: 51,200 events or 50 MB; warnings after 10,240 events or 10 MB
metrics.interpretation: Long-lived projects must shard per work item and roll/continue executions; one immortal project workflow is unsafe.

metrics.value: Temporal Activities and NATS JetStream are at least once; AWS Express is at least once; AWS states Standard state executions are exactly once unless Retry is configured
metrics.interpretation: Every external mutation still needs an idempotency key/outbox or dedupe record; do not infer global exactly-once side effects.
Unsuitable as the sole durable host for days-long approvals; use Standard or another durable workflow.

metrics.value: 1,600+ traces, 7 frameworks; 150 traces used to derive taxonomy; 14 modes/3 categories; Cohen's kappa 0.88
1.1-12% accuracy improvement and up to 20% deployment-cost reduction on tested applications
metrics.caveat: authors' preprint results, not a production SLO

metrics.value: Measure queue age p50/p95, run success without human rescue, retries per step, duplicate-effect rate, escalation rate, tokens/$/wall time per accepted change, revert rate, escaped defects, security-policy denials, and marginal quality versus a single-agent baseline.

reference_workflow: 1. Normalize triggers from issue/PR/comment/schedule/alert/webhook [S24] into an immutable work_item with tenant, repo, commit/base SHA, requested outcome, risk class, budget, provenance, and idempotency key. Validate signatures and treat text as untrusted [S23,S25].

2. A deterministic admission service applies allowlists, concurrency quotas, cost/risk limits, dependency locks, and deduplication. Reject, quarantine, or request clarification before any model/tool call.

3. Persist desired state and append an audit event; start one durable workflow per work item. Store payloads/artifacts in object storage and references/hashes in workflow state to avoid history growth [S3,S4].

4. Route first to the cheapest capable single agent. Invoke a multi-agent branch only for predefined reasons: independent decomposition, specialist boundary, adversarial review, uncertainty threshold, or failed single-agent attempt [S7,S21]. The router emits reason, candidates, confidence, and budget—not only free text.

5. Planner produces a typed DAG: steps, owners/capabilities, inputs/outputs schemas, dependencies, acceptance tests, maximum attempts, timeout/heartbeat, side-effect class, and approval requirement. Deterministic code validates graph acyclicity and policy.

6. Dispatch ready nodes through capability/version-specific queues [S1]. Pin model, prompt, tool/image, repository SHA, dependency lockfile, and policy versions. Use leases/heartbeats so only one active supervisor owns a partition [S16].

7. Worker runs in an ephemeral least-privilege sandbox. It receives only scoped credentials and a clean checkout. All network, shell, file, and remote-agent calls pass a policy proxy. MCP/A2A identity is mapped to local authorization, not trusted from prose [S14,S23].

8. Save structured outputs and artifacts separately. Checkpoint only minimal thread state; keep cross-run memory in a governed store with namespace, provenance, confidence, TTL, ACL, and deletion [S6]. Never use raw chat transcript as authoritative project state.

9. At each external side effect, use work_item/step/attempt idempotency keys. Write an intent/outbox before dispatch, record the remote receipt/result, and reconcile unknown outcomes before retry because acknowledged execution can be lost [S5,S17].

10. Retry only classified transient failures with capped exponential backoff and jitter; send invalid input, policy denial, deterministic test failure, budget exhaustion, and repeated model failure to clarification, replan, quarantine, or dead-letter paths [S2,S19,S26]. Compensate reversible effects; never blindly replay merge/deploy/payment/secret rotation.

11. Join branches in deterministic code. Require schema checks, tests, static/security scans, diff limits, provenance, and an independent reviewer. Voting is useful only when answers are independently sampled and an objective verifier exists [S20,S22].

12. Interrupt for a human at ambiguous requirements, privileged tool expansion, high-risk/security/dependency/license change, failing/non-deterministic verification, production deploy, destructive migration, or exceeded budget. Persist the approval principal, exact artifact hash, scope, and expiry; changing the artifact invalidates approval.

13. Submit PR rather than direct push. Reconcile desired state ('approved SHA deployed and healthy') with actual repository/CI/deployment state in a controller loop [S15]. Rebase and rerun checks if base SHA changes.

14. Deploy canary after approval; observe error/latency/security/business SLOs. On breach, halt downstream work, rollback, open an incident, and attach trace/event history. Do not ask a compromised or failing agent to approve itself.

15. Close with immutable outcome labels and cost/latency/retry/escalation metrics. Curate only reviewed facts into long-term memory. Replay traces in offline evals before changing router/prompts/policies, then canary the control-plane version.

integration_points.intake: GitHub/GitLab issue, PR, review, comment and Actions/webhook events; observability alert/incident bus; scheduled dependency/security work [S24].
integration_points.orchestration: Temporal SDK/service and task queues, Step Functions API/EventBridge, or equivalent durable workflow; Prefect for lower-criticality Python-native flows [S1-S5,S18,S19,S26].
integration_points.transport: NATS JetStream/Kafka/cloud queues using envelope fields event_id, correlation_id, causation_id, tenant, schema_version, producer, timestamp, trace context, payload hash and delivery attempt [S17].
integration_points.agents: LangGraph/MAF/OpenAI SDK embedded as bounded decision activities; A2A 1.0 for remote agents and MCP for scoped tools [S6-S14,S23].
integration_points.state: SQL/transactional workflow store for canonical lifecycle; object/artifact store for patches/logs; vector/search store only as derived memory; secrets manager; policy engine; dedupe/outbox table.
integration_points.engineering: Git hosting API, CI checks, code scanners, package registries, sandbox/container service, deployment controller, feature flags and rollback system.
integration_points.observability: OpenTelemetry-style traces keyed by work item/attempt plus immutable workflow history. Capture routing, model/prompt/tool versions, token/cost, queue time, handoffs, policy decisions, approvals and artifact hashes; redact prompts/secrets. OpenAI built-in traces omit ZDR organizations [S13].

human_gates.when: missing acceptance criteria, ambiguous target, external request, or low-confidence risk classification
human_gates.why: prevents an incorrect plan from multiplying across agents

human_gates.when: new repository, write scope, network domain, secret, production role, MCP/A2A peer, or sandbox exception
human_gates.why: model routing must not grant authority; MCP lists confused-deputy/token/session risks [S23]

human_gates.when: security/auth/billing/data migration/dependency-license/public API or large/high-blast-radius diff
human_gates.why: objective impact cannot be inferred reliably from agent consensus [S20]

human_gates.when: protected branch and any production deployment until local evidence proves bounded auto-merge risk
human_gates.why: approval binds a reviewed artifact hash; new commit invalidates it

human_gates.when: dead-letter, conflicting agent conclusions, flaky test, repeated retry, budget/time cap, unknown side-effect result or SLO regression
human_gates.why: break retry loops and protect external state

human_gates.when: changing prompt/model/router/tool permissions, retry limits, eval threshold or memory schema
human_gates.why: control-plane change can affect every future task; use offline replay plus canary

failure_modes: Supervisor single point of semantic failure: wrong decomposition/routing or premature stop propagates to every worker; recursive delegation can create cycles or unbounded fan-out [S20].

Coordination failures: ambiguous roles, context loss at handoff, agents ignoring others, conformity/groupthink, conflicting edits, stale base SHA, lock contention, and no objective termination/verification [S20-S22].

Distributed-systems failures: duplicate/redelivered jobs, lost acknowledgment after effect, poison messages, out-of-order events, split-brain supervisors, lease expiry during a long call, retry storms, queue starvation, dead-letter neglect, partial joins and compensation failure [S5,S16-S19].

Replay/state failures: non-deterministic workflow code, oversized histories, schema/version mismatch, corrupt checkpoint, incompatible deployment, in-memory checkpoint loss, unbounded retention [S3,S4,S6].
Memory failures: stale/poisoned/private facts, cross-tenant leakage, retrieval amplifying earlier mistakes, no provenance/deletion, vector store treated as truth.

Security failures: prompt injection through issues/repos/tool output, confused deputy, credential/token forwarding, SSRF, malicious MCP/A2A peer or GitHub Action, secret leakage in traces, tool-call argument substitution, supply-chain code execution [S23,S25].

Control/economic failures: runaway model/tool loops, correlated reviewers sharing the same blind spot, expensive multi-agent work on easy tasks, rate limits, vendor outage/lock-in, trace gaps under ZDR, and framework churn (AutoGen entered maintenance mode) [S7,S9,S13,S20,S21].
Product failures: technically passing but unwanted change, benchmark gaming, silent behavior regression, noisy autonomous PRs, ownership diffusion, and reviewers habituated to approving agent output.
controls_and_mitigations: Separate planes: deterministic scheduler/policy/state/authorization/reconciliation in the control plane; LLMs only propose typed plans, routing hints, patches, reviews, and explanations.

Use durable per-item workflow history, versioned schemas, transactional outbox/inbox, idempotency keys, dedupe TTL, capped backoff+jitter, explicit retryable error taxonomy, dead-letter ownership, timeouts/heartbeats, and reconciliation of unknown effects [S2-S5,S17-S19,S26].

Enforce least-privilege short-lived credentials per step, sandbox isolation, egress/domain allowlists, read/write separation, protected branches, signed artifacts, dependency/action pinning, two-person approval for sensitive changes, and no token passthrough [S23,S25].

Bound recursion, fan-out, wall time, tokens, dollars, files/lines changed, tool calls, concurrent jobs and memory retrieval. Circuit-break by repo/model/provider/tool and provide a global kill switch.

Require machine-verifiable contracts: JSON schemas, acceptance tests, static/type/security/license scans, deterministic joins, independent review, confidence/calibration thresholds and fail-closed policies. Agent agreement is evidence, not authorization [S20-S22].

Keep canonical state relational/event-sourced. For memory, require tenant/user namespace, source URI/artifact hash, observation time, confidence, TTL, ACL, PII class, review status and deletion. Quarantine untrusted content; never execute retrieved instructions.

Trace every state transition, routing/handoff/tool/policy decision and approval with correlation/causation IDs, while redacting and limiting retention. Maintain an alternate local audit path when vendor tracing is incompatible with ZDR [S13].
Use Kubernetes-style reconciliation and leased leader election rather than one-shot agents [S15,S16]. Merge only reviewed SHA; deploy canary; auto-rollback and freeze on SLO/security regressions.

maturity_assessment.production_ready: Durable workflow engines, queues, idempotent activities, retry/backoff, event triggers, checkpoint stores, controller reconciliation, leases, sandboxed CI, audit and human approval are mature when operated as normal distributed systems [S1-S6,S15-S19,S24,S25].
maturity_assessment.conditionally_useful: Explicit agent graphs, specialist handoffs, parallel independent review, and A2A 1.0 are useful for bounded, observable tasks with objective verification and budgets [S7-S14,S22]. Framework capability is verified; reliability remains application-specific.
maturity_assessment.emerging: Learned/dynamic routing, shared long-term agent memory, cross-vendor remote-agent ecosystems, automatic plan repair and hybrid SAS/MAS cascades. Evidence is mainly documentation and preprints [S14,S20,S21].
maturity_assessment.speculative: An open-ended LLM supervisor safely owning backlog, permissions, merge, deploy and self-modification with minimal human oversight. MAST failure evidence and missing neutral longitudinal SLOs argue against production trust [S20].

build_vs_buy.buy_managed: Use Temporal Cloud or AWS Step Functions where operational burden and compliance fit; managed Git/CI, secrets, policy, artifact storage and observability reduce undifferentiated work. Validate tenancy, history/retention, egress, regional, ZDR and cost constraints [S4,S13,S18].
build_vs_buy.build_on_open_source: Self-host Temporal plus LangGraph or MAF when portability/custom execution or data control matters. Prefer MAF for new Microsoft-stack work because AutoGen is maintenance-only [S8-S10]. Use NATS/Kafka only as transport, not as the whole orchestrator [S17].
build_vs_buy.custom_required: Admission/risk model, typed work-item schema, repo capability registry, router policy, idempotency/outbox integration, artifact approval binding, memory governance, eval corpus, SLO dashboards, kill switches and organization-specific gates.
build_vs_buy.avoid: A new bespoke scheduler/retry database unless scale/compliance makes established engines impossible; chat-only multi-agent frameworks as the system of record; direct autonomous production credentials; starting new AutoGen projects [S9].

recommended_pattern.name: Durable controller with bounded agent activities and selective fan-out
recommended_pattern.architecture: One authoritative durable workflow per work item; conventional queue workers; canonical SQL/event history; immutable artifact store; Kubernetes-style reconciler for repository/deploy desired state; sandbox/policy proxy; checkpointed agent graph only inside bounded activities; governed memory; complete audit and evaluation plane.
recommended_pattern.routing: Single-agent first. Fan out only when predicted uncertainty/risk/complexity exceeds a calibrated threshold or when independent verification has known value. Cap branches and use deterministic aggregation. Fall back to human, not endless agent debate [S7,S20-S22].
recommended_pattern.rollout: Phase 1 read-only triage and plans. Phase 2 agent PRs with mandatory review. Phase 3 low-risk auto-merge after local SLO/eval thresholds. Phase 4 canary deploy and reversible remediation. Never grant broader rights merely because benchmark score improves.
recommended_pattern.technology_choice: Choose the durable engine before the agent framework. As of 2026-09-13, Temporal is the strongest general fit for long waits/recovery/custom workers; Step Functions fits AWS-native workflows; LangGraph/MAF add agent-local graphs and checkpoint/HITL. Use A2A at trust boundaries only with authenticated peers and local policy [S1-S14,S18-S19].
recommended_pattern.decision_rule: Keep a multi-agent path only if an A/B comparison against the best single-agent baseline improves accepted-change rate or reduces escapes enough to cover added token, latency, coordination failures and operations.

open_questions: What accepted-change, rollback, escaped-defect, security and human-minutes SLOs do these architectures sustain over 6-12 months on real repositories? No neutral longitudinal comparison was found.
How should routers be calibrated under model drift, task distribution shift and sparse ground truth, and how much of [S21]'s hybrid gain transfers to software maintenance?
Can A2A 1.0 implementations deliver consistent idempotency, authorization, cancellation, retention, provenance and conformance across vendors, beyond wire-level interoperability [S14]?
How can memory poisoning, provenance, revocation/right-to-delete and cross-agent/tenant access be evaluated with standard benchmarks?
What is the safest migration and replay/versioning method for in-flight workflows when prompts, models, tools, schemas or workflow code change [S3,S6]?
Which failures are decorrelated by independent agents versus repeated because models share training data, prompts, tools and evaluators [S20,S22]?
What cost/latency frontier justifies a durable multi-agent branch versus a stronger single model, and how stable are vendor-reported delivery/exactly-once semantics end to end [S5,S17,S18]?

sources.title: Task Queues
supported_claims: Temporal task queues are dynamically allocated and polled by workers; activity, workflow, and Nexus task queues separate dispatch from workers.

sources.title: What is a Temporal Retry Policy?
supported_claims: Activity retries are automatic by default and retry behavior is declarative; workflow failures are treated differently.

sources.title: Events and Event History
supported_claims: Temporal appends workflow events to history and uses replay to recover after crashes.

sources.title: Workflow Execution limits
supported_claims: A workflow history is limited to 51,200 events or 50 MB, with warnings at 10,240 events or 10 MB.

sources.title: Error handling - Python SDK
supported_claims: Activities follow at-least-once execution and therefore should use idempotency keys; a worker can finish an action then crash before acknowledgment, causing retry.

sources.title: Persistence
supported_claims: LangGraph checkpointers store thread-scoped checkpoints for continuity, interruption, time travel, and fault tolerance; stores hold cross-thread long-term memory.
In-memory savers do not survive restarts and production needs a persistent saver; checkpoints need retention.

sources.title: Multi-agent
supported_claims: LangChain documents subagents, handoffs, skills, router, and custom workflows, while warning that a single agent with suitable tools can often produce similar results.

sources.title: Microsoft Agent Framework repository README
supported_claims: MAF provides Python/.NET graph workflows with sequential, concurrent, handoff, and group patterns plus checkpointing, streaming, human-in-loop, time travel, OpenTelemetry, and a separate durable extension.

sources.title: AutoGen repository README
sources.publication_update_date: repository active as of 2026-09-12; maintenance-mode notice current at access
supported_claims: AutoGen is in maintenance mode, gets no new features, and directs new users to Microsoft Agent Framework 1.0 and existing users to migrate.

sources.title: Agent Runtime Environments
supported_claims: AutoGen Core defines standalone and distributed runtimes for communication, identities, lifecycle, and security/privacy boundaries.

sources.title: Handoffs
supported_claims: OpenAI Agents SDK represents delegation handoffs as model-visible tools and permits input filtering/customization.

sources.title: Guardrails
supported_claims: Input and output guardrails can block a run, but parallel input checks may finish after the expensive model has started; workflow boundary semantics matter.

sources.title: Tracing
supported_claims: The SDK traces generations, tool calls, handoffs, guardrails, and custom events by default; tracing is unavailable under OpenAI Zero Data Retention policy.

sources.title: Agent2Agent (A2A) Protocol Specification 1.0.0
sources.publisher_author: A2A Project / Linux Foundation Agentic AI Foundation
supported_claims: A2A 1.0 supplies Agent Cards, task/message/artifact data models, task lifecycle, polling/streaming/push updates, authenticated discovery, and long-running human-in-loop interactions across opaque agents.

sources.title: Controllers
supported_claims: Kubernetes controllers continuously compare actual with desired state and act to reconcile differences.

sources.title: Leases
supported_claims: Lease objects support heartbeats and leader election, a useful mechanism for singleton supervisors and liveness.

sources.title: JetStream
supported_claims: JetStream persists and replays messages and provides at-least-once delivery with server-side streams and stateful consumers.

sources.title: Choosing workflow type in Step Functions
supported_claims: AWS states Standard workflows have exactly-once state execution unless Retry is configured and retained history, whereas Express workflows can run up to five minutes and use at-least-once execution.

sources.title: Handling errors in Step Functions workflows
supported_claims: Step Functions supports typed retry/catch policies with interval, maximum attempts, backoff, and jitter controls.

sources.title: Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?
sources.source_type: independent academic preprint; annotated empirical study
supported_claims: MAST-Data contains 1,600+ traces across seven frameworks; taxonomy development used 150 traces, found 14 failure modes in three categories, and reported inter-annotator kappa 0.88.
Reported benchmark gains from MAS are often minimal and failures cluster in system design, inter-agent misalignment, and task verification.

sources.title: Single-agent or Multi-agent Systems? Why Not Both?
supported_claims: The study reports diminishing MAS benefits with stronger frontier models and a hybrid request-cascading design yielding 1.1-12% accuracy improvement while reducing deployment costs by up to 20% across its tested applications.

sources.title: More Agents Is All You Need
supported_claims: Sampling-and-voting performance increased with agent count in tested benchmarks, with gains related to task difficulty; this is a narrow ensemble result, not proof that arbitrary collaborative topologies improve.

sources.title: Security Best Practices
supported_claims: MCP guidance identifies confused-deputy risks, token passthrough, SSRF, local server compromise, session hijacking, and scope-minimization requirements.

sources.title: Events that trigger workflows
supported_claims: Repository events such as issues, pull requests, comments, schedules, and workflow dispatch can trigger control-plane intake.

sources.title: Secure use reference
supported_claims: GitHub warns that untrusted workflow input and compromised actions can expose secrets and recommends least privilege, pinning actions, and review controls.

sources.title: How to automatically rerun your workflow when it fails
supported_claims: Prefect flows and tasks expose retry count, delays, exponential backoff, jitter, and conditional retry controls.

confidence.overall: High for distributed-systems/control-plane primitives and current official framework/protocol status; medium for recommended composition; low-to-medium for claims of multi-agent performance and economics.
confidence.high: Temporal/NATS/AWS delivery and limits, LangGraph persistence semantics, A2A 1.0 surface, Kubernetes controller/lease patterns, AutoGen maintenance status—direct specifications/docs/repositories [S1-S19].
confidence.medium: That a deterministic durable controller plus bounded agents is the best reference pattern. It is an engineering synthesis strongly supported by mature primitives and observed failure classes but lacks a neutral head-to-head production trial.
confidence.low_medium: Transfer of MAST, hybrid cascade and Agent Forest results to long-running software projects because [S20-S22] are preprints/benchmark studies and not longitudinal production evidence.
confidence.claim_labels: Entries explicitly label verified documentation, vendor claims, independent findings, inference and unknowns; vendor 'production-ready' and 'exactly-once' language is not treated as independent proof.

conflicts.claim_a: More agents/sampling-and-voting improves accuracy with scale [S22].
conflicts.claim_b: MAS gains are often minimal and have 14 recurrent failure modes [S20]; benefits diminish with stronger base models [S21].
conflicts.resolution: Topology and verification explain much of the difference. Independent samples with objective voting differ from conversational dependency chains. Use selective fan-out and local A/B evidence.

conflicts.claim_a: Microsoft calls MAF 1.0 production-ready and successor to AutoGen [S8,S9].
conflicts.claim_b: Feature presence and repository activity do not prove application SLOs; its durable execution is partly a separate extension [S8].
conflicts.resolution: Treat release/status as verified vendor facts but operational reliability as unverified; pair with a proven durable engine until tested.

conflicts.claim_a: AWS calls Standard workflows exactly once [S18].
conflicts.claim_b: Temporal/NATS document at-least-once execution and duplicate-effect scenarios [S5,S17].
conflicts.resolution: These refer to different boundaries. A state transition can be exactly-once while an external API outcome remains unknown. Design all effects idempotently and reconcile.

conflicts.claim_a: Agent SDK guardrails can terminate unsafe runs [S12].
conflicts.claim_b: Parallel guardrails may allow costly work to start and boundary guardrails do not replace per-tool authorization [S12,S23].
conflicts.resolution: Use blocking admission for high-risk input and deterministic authorization on every capability/tool call.
